definition: Aggressive orders arriving at a price without moving it, because resting size is taking the other side. It describes what the tape shows rather than who is behind it: one large passive seller and a queue of small ones print the same thing. Opposite of exhaustion.

The market maker’s problem: the orders that hit a resting quote are more likely to come from someone who knows something. It is the reason the spread exists at all, and the reason it widens when the chance of an informed counterparty rises.
The lowest price a seller is willing to accept. The "sell side" of the order book.
Volatility indicator measuring average price range over a period (typically 14 bars). Used for stop-loss placement and position sizing.

Running a rule over past prices to see what it would have done. Lesson 63 treats a backtest as evidence with a strength that can be stated rather than as a result, and prices the four subtractions between a gross figure and one worth believing.

The share of candidates that are genuinely alive before any test is run. It is the input nobody can measure and the one that decides what a passing test is worth: at one candidate in ten, a disciplined test leaves 43.2 per cent of what it accepts real, and two ordinary habits take that to 6.0.

One hundredth of one per cent. Costs are quoted in basis points so that instruments at different prices can be compared: a penny of spread is 0.97 basis points on a share near 103 and 4.17 on one near 48.
The highest price a buyer is willing to pay. The "buy side" of the order book.
The difference between the highest bid and lowest ask. Represents the cost of immediacy (market orders). Widens with volatility/uncertainty, tightens with confidence.

What it costs to borrow a security in order to sell it short, plus the risk that the lender recalls it. Lesson 82 concedes it is the one price the course never measured, and it is the whole bill for the short leg of a spread.
When price breaks a significant swing high (in uptrend) or swing low (in downtrend), confirming trend continuation. Part of market structure analysis.
When price moves through a defined level (resistance, range high, consolidation). It either continues or reverses, and nothing visible at the moment of the break tells you which.

The size at which a rule’s own impact eats its edge. Lesson 68 turns that into a number for one rule and finds two thirds of the edge spent to collect the other third at the largest position it can hold.
When price breaks counter-trend structure, signaling potential trend reversal. Weaker than BOS.
Automated trading system safeguard that halts trading when predefined conditions are met (max loss, volatility spike, drawdown threshold). Also called kill switch.

How alike two series move, between −1 and 1. It is the single input that decides how many independent bets a set of positions amounts to, and lesson 74 shows it moves enough between two halves of one record to change the answer.

The correlation between two different instruments, as opposed to between two rules on the same one. Lesson 82 shows four long positions across two instruments carry two full bets only if it is below 0.06, and that turning one leg over is worth more than adding the instrument.
Running total of delta (buy volume minus sell volume) over time. Shows net buying or selling pressure.
Private exchange for institutional trading, not visible on public order books. Large block orders executed off-exchange to minimize market impact.
The difference between buy volume and sell volume at a specific price level or time period. Positive delta = more buying than selling.

When price makes a new high/low but an indicator (RSI, momentum, volume) does not. The indicator is a function of the same prices, so a divergence is an arithmetic consequence of the path rather than an independent witness to it.

The distance from a peak in the equity curve to the lowest point after it, quoted in R or in per cent. Lesson 67 puts the depth you should expect on an edge you believe in, and finds an eight-R line switches off 59.5 per cent of the systems that genuinely work.

The average result of one trade, in R, after costs. It is a quantity to be measured rather than felt: lesson 18 shows what an edge of a tenth of an R actually looks like from inside, which is mostly like nothing.
When aggressive buying/selling moves price but no one absorbs the orders, causing rapid price movement. Opposite of absorption. Often precedes reversals.
Win rate times average win, less loss rate times average loss. It is the one number that decides whether a method makes money, and every cost in this course is subtracted from it.
Chart type showing volume traded at each price level within each candle, split by bid/ask. Reveals order flow and absorption/exhaustion patterns.

The number of trades you fix, before the first one, as the point at which you will judge the record. Lesson 65 shows that judging continuously instead takes a dead system’s pass rate from 5.05 per cent to 24.25.
The price movement your own order causes. It grows with size faster than the spread does, roughly as size to the power of one and a half, which is why a rule that works small can stop working large.

What a set of correlated positions actually amounts to: the count divided by one plus the count less one times the average correlation. Two rules at a correlation of 0.88 are 1.06 bets rather than two, and the ceiling as you add positions is one over the correlation.
Large orders placed by institutions (hedge funds, banks, prop firms). Characterized by absorption, dark pool activity, and gradual accumulation/distribution.
Automated trading safeguard that immediately stops all trading and/or closes positions when triggered by predefined conditions (max loss, drawdown, volatility).

The delay between a decision and its arrival at the market. Lesson 69 prices five minutes between signal and order at 32.10 basis points on one instrument, which is more than a second venue gives back across a whole record.

Orders that have not executed yet. They are not spread evenly across the price axis but pile up at levels you can name in advance, and lesson 25 shows the piling needs no coordination: everyone arrives at the same level by the same reasoning.

A concentration of resting orders at one level, common at round numbers and just beyond swing highs and lows. A stop is invisible until it fires, so a pool is a quantity of certain future flow at a known price that nobody can observe beforehand.

A break of a level that triggers the stops resting there, followed by a reversal. A cascade through resting stops needs no author, and lesson 27 sets out both what deliberate conduct actually consists of and why it cannot be identified from price.

A participant who quotes both sides and earns the spread for supplying immediacy. Lesson 53 works out what that spread has to cover: inventory risk, the cost of being adversely selected, and the fee schedule.
The pattern of swing highs and lows that defines trend direction. Higher highs + higher lows = uptrend. Lower highs + lower lows = downtrend.
List of all pending buy (bid) and sell (ask) orders at different price levels. Depth of Market (DOM). Shows liquidity and imbalances.
The sequence and volume of buy and sell orders executed in real-time. Reveals institutional activity, absorption/exhaustion, and momentum shifts.
Optimizing trading strategy parameters too specifically to historical data, causing it to fail in live trading. Curve-fitting.
The share of a period’s volume your own order represents. It sets the trade-off lesson 57 solves: go faster and pay impact, go slower and carry exposure for longer.
The price level with the most traded volume in a period. It is the mode of a binned distribution, so it moves with the bin width: lesson 29 measures it sliding 9.5 ticks across a 15-tick day.
The total risk open at once, as a share of the account: positions times risk per trade. Lesson 72 prices the day on which every stop hits together, which is the day heat was defined to survive.

The chance a test accepts a system that genuinely works. Lesson 84’s bar over 156 trades has a power of 0.3461 against an edge of a tenth of an R, which means a real edge fails that test about two times in three.

Gross profit divided by gross loss. Lesson 70 turns it into the bar a filter has to clear: on a profit factor of 3.27, a filter equally good in both directions must be right about 76.6 per cent of unseen trades to help at all.

One unit of risk: the distance from entry to the stop, times size. Everything after lesson 20 is quoted in it so that trades of different sizes can be added. Lesson 85 shows the unit itself moves, by a factor of 2.711 between two halves of one record.
Current market state: trending (directional), ranging (choppy), or volatile (high ATR). Determines how to interpret indicators.

When an indicator changes its historical signals after the fact, so a backtest reads a chart the trader could never have seen. Lesson 49 shows how to test any indicator for it yourself rather than take an assurance.

The chance a sequence of losses takes the account below the point it can recover from. It falls fast with a smaller fraction risked per trade and rises fast with a longer losing run than the one you planned for.

One entry and one exit, and therefore the unit every cost in this course is charged in. Lesson 63 prices one at 0.1230 a share, and lesson 83 splits that into the part a second venue can compete for and the part that is a delay.
Momentum oscillator (0-100). Traditional interpretation: >70 = overbought, <30 = oversold. Reality: regime-dependent (continuation in trends, reversal in ranges).
The difference between expected fill price and actual fill price. Caused by fast markets, low liquidity, or market orders. Must be included in backtests.

A label for institutional participants. Lesson 9 names who is actually in the room and what each is optimising for, which is more useful than a two-way split, and lesson 27 finds that the conduct actually proved in court runs at institutional size against other machines.

An instruction that becomes a market order when price trades through a level. It is not resting in the book and nobody can see it, and when it fires it asks for whatever price exists rather than the one you named.
See Liquidity Sweep. Brief break of a level to trigger stops before reversing.
Real-time feed of every executed trade showing time, price, volume, and aggressor side (buy/sell). Used for order flow analysis.
A mean divided by its standard error. It is a ratio, so it does not change when the unit does: lesson 63’s 3.65 is 3.65 in dollars, in R, and in either half of the record’s own R.

The upper boundary of the value area. The 70 per cent is a convention borrowed from one standard deviation of a normal distribution, and the box labelled 70 per cent holds between 70 and 84 per cent of the session depending on how it was binned.
The lower boundary of the value area. An interval is a steadier summary than the point of control — 3.5 ticks of movement against 9.5 — which is the reason to read it instead.

A loss size a period is not expected to exceed at a stated probability. Lesson 75 reads it beside the other limits and asks which one binds first, which is the only question a set of limits actually answers.

The variance of a multi-bar change divided by the number of bars times the variance of a one-bar change. One means a random walk and below one means the series turns; lesson 85 measures 0.3434 over sixty closes.
Histogram showing volume traded at each price level over a time period. Identifies POC, VAH, VAL, and high/low volume nodes.

Average price weighted by volume. Institutions use it as an execution benchmark, which is what lesson 57 prices when it works a million shares against it. Nothing in this course establishes it as a level price is drawn back to.
Backtesting method that trains on Period 1, tests on Period 2, trains on Period 2, tests on Period 3, etc. Prevents overfitting by validating across different market regimes.

The share of trades that finish positive. On its own it says nothing: lesson 4 shows a $2 spread on a $2.50 stop needs a 90 per cent win rate to break even, and lesson 17 shows why the average sizes matter as much as the count.
